Pele Yoetz 382:3: And behold, what they said (Shabbat 54b), "Whoever has the power to protest against the people of his city is held accountable for the people of his city; against the people of his household, is held accountable for the people of his household" - this implies that the matter is not said of everyone, but only of one who has the power to protest. And so they said regarding the verse (Deuteronomy 1:13), "and their guilt (va'asimem) shall be upon your heads" - it is written "va'ashamam" (and their guilt), that the guilt of the community rests upon the heads of the community, that is, regarding the matter of forceful protest (mecha'ah), for rebuke (tochachah) is one thing and forceful protest is another: rebuke is with words, and forceful protest is with rods and staves, which is not in every person's power, but rather every man rules in his own house, and the heads of the communities govern their communities and have the power to break the jaws of the wicked - upon them rests the obligation of forceful protest; but the obligation of rebuke is a matter equal for every soul.
Pele Yoetz 382:4: And indeed, through sin, flattery has grown strong, and in this generation there is none who rebukes, especially not a respected man - if he sees him transgressing the words of Torah, he is ashamed and afraid to approach and say to him, "Why do you transgress the commandment of the King, the King of the universe," and he presses his face into the ground and makes himself as one who did not see and did not know. Woe to us from the day of judgment and the day of rebuke, for when the Name calls to account the commandment of rebuke, what shall we answer and what shall we say, for He will say, "You were very insistent on your own honor, and how much more so on the honor of your father and mother - had you seen a man striking your father and mother or cursing them, you would have gone forth to meet him with weapons and fought him even unto his life; why then did you not insist on the honor of Heaven when you saw a man transgressing a sin, one who treats the honor of Heaven lightly, causing grief and anger and blemish, and a talebearer separates close friends, and many such evils, with no man taking it to heart - would that he not rejoice at his fellow's misfortune, so that he himself be honored and his fellow disgraced." And there are those who do not rebuke because in this generation there is none who will accept rebuke - for if a man wishes to rebuke people like himself, the scoffers will mock him and say, "Who made you a ruler and judge and rebuker," and they insult and demean him. And regarding such people, it is a mitzvah not to rebuke them, for they said (Yevamot 65b), "Just as it is a mitzvah to say a thing that will be heeded, so it is a mitzvah not to say a thing that will not be heeded." And there is also a prohibition against rebuking them, as it is written (Proverbs 9:8), "Do not rebuke a scoffer." But a person cannot simply say, "I am certain they will not listen or that they are scoffers," for the Lord looks to the heart, and if it is revealed before Him, is it revealed before us - unless it is as clear as the sun that he pays no heed to the forbidden and will not listen to the voice of whisperers, for then they said (Beitzah 30a), "It is better that they be unwitting sinners than deliberate ones." And this applies specifically when they do not know that it is a sin, so that they are unwitting; but if they know it is a sin and transgress it anyway, he should rebuke them to their face, perhaps they will turn from their evil way, for in that case it is not applicable to say, "It is better that they be unwitting."
Pele Yoetz 382:5: But even for a good purpose there is a limit, for even in rebuke he should not multiply words excessively if he fears they will not accept it - for Aaron was punished for taking the calf and slaughtering it before them, showing them that there was nothing substantial to it (Vayikra Rabbah 7:1), in a manner that turned them into willful sinners. And so they wrote that before the public one should rebuke only once, and before the public the principle "better that they be unwitting" does not apply, so that he should speak to a hundred, and if not, at least to one. And regarding a matter whose prohibition is explicit in the Torah, we do not say "better that they be unwitting," but rather he is obligated to inform them and rebuke them.
Pele Yoetz 382:6: And one must be careful in the manner of rebuke so as not to bear sin because of it - namely, that he not shame his fellow, and not speak harshly to him in a way that would lead to strife and quarrel and hatred and rivalry, but rather "a soft tongue breaks a bone" (Proverbs 25:15), and in private. And how greatly must preachers be careful not to touch upon people's honor, and not to mention within their sermon a sin that some specific individual has committed, for that preacher shall be considered as one who has shed blood; but even when he rebukes concerning transgressions that particular individuals have grown accustomed to, he should first honor and elevate the person so that he will accept the rebuke - and this is how the commentators explained the verse (ibid. 9:8), "Do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you; rebuke a wise man, and he will love you" - that one should not rebuke in the language of a scoffer, saying to him, "You wicked scoffer, why do you do such and such," but rather he should say, "You are wise, a good man, praised and glorified, and such deeds are not fitting for you; turn from this, so that you may be complete in all things and your deeds be praised in the gates." And if he does not accept blessings and does not turn from his evil way, let him speak harshly and go further, even to striking him, if he has the power to enforce it. And it is best for a preacher, when he sees that people are lax in some matter, to seek to expound from a book on that very topic, or, when standing before a congregation, to steer his words to make known the prohibition in that matter and its severity - let the one who will listen, listen, and let the one who will desist, desist.
Pele Yoetz 382:7: And this commandment a person can fulfill even after his death for many generations, if the Name has granted him understanding, by being recorded in a book of laws and ethical instruction. And even though there are already many such books, and Torah is offered in a corner with none seeking or asking for it except the remnant few, nevertheless let him do so and let his Torah be recorded, for perhaps in the course of many days it will be found that someone takes his book in hand and his words bear fruit for him, and he too will build from it, and his lips will move in the grave. And therefore how good and pleasant it would be to compose a book of laws and ethics in the vernacular for those who do not know the holy tongue, for the common people are now numerous, and it is more beneficial and meritorious for one's soul to compose such books than to compose books of dialectics and clever novellae and sermons, of which there are already many, lying rolled up in the dust, eaten by moths, for the books are many and the students are few, and they content themselves with the books of the Talmud and halachic authorities, and the early commentators and digests of laws - would that the time suffice us to study even these properly - but for those who rebuke, it shall be pleasant, and upon them shall come the blessing of good.
Pele Yoetz 383:1: Tikkun (Rectification) - We have already written that every person must rectify what he has distorted, for if he does not do so, he will surely be punished for not having had regard for the honor of his Maker. And there are already books full of splendor that speak of a specific rectification appointed for each sin, and for each limb with which he sinned and formed bundles of transgressions, he should perform corresponding bundles of commandments - perhaps there is hope that he will be reconciled to his Master, and He will heal him. And likewise he should rectify his distortion through fasts, self-mortifications, and acts of charity as much as he can bear. And he need not strive to rectify only his own sins, but must also rectify the sins of the community and the sins of all Israel, and especially the iniquities of his ancestors, as it is written (Leviticus 26:40), "And they shall confess their iniquity and the iniquity of their fathers." And with every good deed he performs, and with every affliction he undertakes, and with every act of charity he gives, he should have the intention, and even say aloud, that he does it for the atonement of his own sins and the sins of his ancestors and the sins of all Israel, and that his deeds be favorable before the Name for the rectification of his own soul, spirit, and neshamah, and for the elevation of the souls of his parents and on behalf of all Israel, for this is like lighting one candle from another - others benefit and he loses nothing. And if he is the head of the community, or among the leaders and notables of the cities, this commandment rests upon them to strive for the betterment of the people of the city, whether in matters of prohibition or matters of money - if they see that the people are lax in some prohibition, let them be strong to stand in the breach and fence in the breaches of the city through enactments, fences, and restrictions, according to the place and the time and the need of the hour. And likewise let them restrict them from excessive expenditure for show, for the Torah has regard for the money of Israel.
Pele Yoetz 383:2: And all the more so must one have regard for the poor of Israel, for when the custom of the city involves certain expenditures, people observe the custom more strictly than the law of the Torah itself, rich and poor alike. And there are destitute poor people who cannot even afford a loaf of bread, and they sell their own clothing in order to fulfill the custom of the region, for they are ashamed and embarrassed to show their poverty and to deviate from the local custom - and so the wretched poor man goes about weeping from his poverty, and it is impossible to say he is exempt from observing the customs of the region, whether in the clothing of his wife and children and her jewelry, or in the practices of social propriety at celebrations and rejoicing, where much money is sunk and thrown away, and this is a bad custom even for the wealthy, who thereby transgress the prohibition of "do not destroy" (bal tashchit) - and instead of spending this money on these bad customs, they could have given it to the poor to revive the hearts of the crushed, which would be counted to them as a great mitzvah. And all the more difficult is this for the poor, who cannot even afford bread to eat and clothing to wear, and when some occasion of joy comes to them, such as a child being born to them or reaching the age of marriage, their joy turns to sorrow for them, for they do not know where to turn for help to find, even temporarily, the funds for the increased expenditure; and if they manage to find something by pawning an item or selling their clothing, it seems to them like a gift and they rejoice as one who finds great spoil, for this preserves their dignity - but when they find nothing at all, then it is exceedingly bitter for them, and because of the excessive expenditure there is even a kind of indirect legal liability, for if the poor man wishes to sell the honor of being a sandak (godfather) or a groomsman, no one will buy it, for the expense exceeds the benefit.
Pele Yoetz 383:3: Regarding all these matters, the leaders of the cities must keep their eyes open, and let us take counsel from the elders - for indeed our sages, of blessed memory, were diligent about the welfare of the poor and made all faces equal, and obligated the wealthy to be lenient regarding their own honor so as not to shame the one who has nothing, as it is written (Ta'anit 31a) that on the fifteenth of Av the daughters of Israel would go out to dance in the vineyards, all of them in borrowed white garments, even the king's daughter, so as not to shame the one who had none. And likewise regarding burial shrouds (Mo'ed Katan 27b), they saw that one who could not afford it would abandon his dead and flee because of the excessive expense that people were accustomed to incur, until the household of Rabban Gamliel came and adopted a humble practice for themselves - and there are many such matters explained in the Talmud.
Pele Yoetz 383:4: And if a person should say, "Let one who has the means do so and increase his expenditures, and one who does not have the means need not do so" - this is impossible, whether because of shame or because of domestic strife, for one woman envies her fellow, and such is the way of women who wish to resemble one another so that all faces be equal, and it is impossible to say that this brings no consequence. And moreover, it becomes burdensome even for the wealthy, and there is also a prohibition in wasting money for vanity and emptiness, and for this too a person will be called to give judgment and reckoning, for the One who gave him his money did not give it to him so that he squander it recklessly, but rather so that he support the members of his household with honor and support others from what is his - not truly his own, but entrusted to him through his hand, for money is a deposit in his hand to fulfill the will of the depositor, and if he spends it on excesses, he is misappropriating the deposit.
Pele Yoetz 383:5: Behold, then, the leaders should change these customs and establish good enactments and upright practices, and likewise they must have regard for the poor and make enactments and set a fixed price ceiling on staple foods and on all kinds of food and drink, so that they not be sold at a high price but only at a small markup, as is explained in the halachic authorities.
Pele Yoetz 383:6: And it is true that at first this will be difficult for many of the common people, and for the women whose understanding is light, and they will weep to their families over the change of customs and speak wrongly of the leaders; but one should not be concerned about this in the face of the good deed and the good reward they will receive from Heaven, and in the end the matter will be loved and cherished and accepted and pleasing to all, and once they are reconciled to it, it will become sweet and pleasant to them. But the leaders of the cities must stand guard, and if a man breaches the fence and transgresses the enactments of the community, they should crush him and pursue him with fines or with blows until excommunication, so that their enactment be established and upheld, and so that not everyone builds his own high place for himself and exalts himself, saying, "I will do as I please and am not bound." And a truly good man will certainly not transgress the enactments of the community even if he must lose a great deal of money, for God stands in the congregation of the mighty; therefore, even if it seems to him in his own judgment that they did not act properly, he should uphold their words and break the jaws of the wicked who wish to transgress their words, for indeed they said (Ecclesiastes 10:8), "and whoever breaches a fence, a serpent shall bite him."
Pele Yoetz 383:7: And especially must enactments and fences be made regarding matters of danger to life, for danger is treated more stringently than a mere prohibition. And likewise enactments must be made to ease the burden on the public, for the honor of the public is great, and the prohibition against burdening the public is severe, overriding even a rabbinic prohibition, as explained in the Talmud (Berachot 19b, Yoma 70a) and in the halachic authorities, and see the final word on this in the book Shalmei Tzibbur. And in all such matters, an obligation rests upon the heads of the children of Israel to search out bad customs that exist and to uproot them gradually, and to make enactments as the need of the hour requires, all with moderation and with pleasant speech, so that they may be accepted, and likewise they should establish for them charitable funds and holy fellowships and study groups and good customs, doing all that is in their power to do - great is the deed, and it merits the many, for the merit of the many depends upon it.
Pele Yoetz 384:1: Tachbulot (Stratagems) - It is written (Proverbs 24:6), "For by wise strategy you shall wage your war." And just as a person employs so many schemes and stratagems for his own honor and to earn money, all the more so must he devise counsel for himself and stratagems in order to wage the obligatory war against the adversary who besets him, for he is an old king, and like a man of war he stirs up jealousy, sounds an alarm, and shrieks against man.
Pele Yoetz 384:2: And behold, for every good thing a person wishes to do, Satan stands at his right hand to oppose him and to withhold good from its rightful owner - for indeed our sages, of blessed memory, said (Berachot 5a), "Let a person incite his good inclination against his evil inclination; if he overcomes it, good, and if not, let him engage in Torah study." And they likewise said (Kiddushin 30b), "If this repulsive one confronts you, drag him to the study house - if he is stone, he shall dissolve; if he is iron, he shall shatter." Behold, then, the adjacent inclination incites him with a double incitement, that he not engage in Torah and that he not go to the study house. And it is likewise written (Isaiah 55:3), "Listen, and your soul shall live," for through diligence in hearing the words of Torah his soul shall live, and the adjacent inclination incites him to turn his ear away from hearing Torah. And they likewise said (Berachot 5b) that he should remember the day of death, and the adjacent inclination incites him that even if he is seventy or eighty years old, he should consider that he will still live another eighty years, and thus he hardens his heart so that he falls into evil, and all such things - and what shall the son do so as not to sin, since the inclination of man's heart is evil from his youth, and it is fire, and we are but flesh and blood - how can we overcome it? This is the counsel that has been counseled: that he employ a stratagem like a man of war, showing himself as though he does not wish to fight, until his enemy despairs of him and settles securely alone, and then suddenly he shall rise against him and strike him down. And so did King David, peace be upon him, do - all day he would say, "To such and such a place I am going, to such and such a dwelling I am going," and through this his inclination would keep its distance from him, and suddenly his feet would lead him to the study house (Yalkut Shimoni, Psalms, remez 890). And therefore it is the custom of the righteous to say little and do much, for indeed they said (Sanhedrin 26b) that thought avails for matters of Torah, and all the more so speech - for if a person merely thinks or says, "I shall study such and such," or "I shall do such and such a good deed," the adjacent inclination stands against him with all its strength, or rolls upon him many obstacles and hindrances to prevent him. Therefore, if his heart stirs with a good thing, let him immediately and at once join the good thought to the deed; if he cannot do it immediately, let him leap and vow to do it, in the manner of what is written (Psalms 119:106), "I have sworn and confirmed it, to keep Your righteous ordinances" - all according to what kind of person he is, let him spur himself on as much as he can.
Pele Yoetz 384:3: And there is yet another great fence and a great stratagem, and it is the teaching of our sages, of blessed memory, who said (Pesachim 50b), "A person should always engage in Torah and mitzvot even not for their own sake, for out of doing so not for their own sake, he comes to do so for their own sake." For when the evil inclination sees someone engaging in a mitzvah not for its own sake, in order to receive a good reward for his effort, it leaves him alone and says, "This one is one of ours, for he is not serving the Name but serving himself, for he acts for his own sake." And the segulah of the Torah is that it is a spice against the evil inclination, and "the commandment of the Lord is pure, enlightening the eyes," and out of not for its own sake, he comes to do it for its own sake. Behold, then, it is good for a man to calculate the reward of a mitzvah as though a man stood before him and placed money in his hand for every good deed and for every word of Torah - so many coins for this, so many coins for that - and with such stratagems shall he wage war with the evil inclination; perhaps he will be able to drive it away from him, and to one who comes to purify himself, the Lord shall help him and be his strength.
Pele Yoetz 385:1: Talmidei Chachamim (Torah Scholars) - Torah scholars must be modest and set apart in their conduct, so that all who see them recognize that they are the seed the Lord has blessed, and they must conduct themselves with piety and fulfill every matter of piety. And even if he wishes to be lenient in some matter due to the need of the hour, he should not be lenient in front of the common people, for they learn from what goes wrong, and not everyone understands their reasoning and explanations and the extenuating circumstances, and it could lead to desecration of the Name. And this is like the teaching of Rabbi Yochanan found in the Talmud (Yoma 86a), who said, "For one such as I, if I walk four cubits without Torah or without tefillin due to circumstances beyond my control, and people do not know this and think I did it out of laxity, there is a desecration of the Name." And Rav said, "For one such as I, if I take meat and do not pay for it immediately, there is a desecration of the Name."
Pele Yoetz 385:2: And Torah scholars must be exceedingly careful to be haters of unjust gain and haters of gifts - that is, they should not pursue the wealthy so that they give them gifts or sell to them cheaply. And they should not buy on credit, and if they did buy on credit, they should hasten to pay, for aside from the fact that if it was given to them under pressure and not willingly there is a taint of robbery in it (Sefer Chasidim, section 316), similar to one who benefits from a meal that does not suffice for its own host, there is furthermore a severe desecration of the Name in this, for people say, "See how sharp the Torah scholars are at extracting money, and their entire concern and aim is to extract money," and they do not wish to know that the scholar is in dire straits and has dependents relying on him. And what shall those who bless and say that they have made the Torah into an axe with which to dig, and that they make use of the crown of Torah - such and such things they say, mocking the messengers of God - though there is some truth in what they say, for what they [the scholars] do is not good, and there is a taint of prohibition in it. And upon whom should they rely? Upon our Father in Heaven, and they shall be reduced in this world. And it is better for them to occupy themselves with heavy labor even if it is beneath their honor, such as being cantors or teachers of small children wherever they can find such positions, and to content themselves with little, and not to burden the wealthy, and not to desecrate the Name of Heaven publicly, God forbid, for it is better for a person to die of hunger than to be wicked before the Omnipresent, and they should not desecrate the Name of Heaven - for a person is recognized by his purse as gold is tested in the furnace, and those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing.
Pele Yoetz 385:3: And Torah scholars must maintain their own dignity, not sitting in the company of the common people, and not engaging in frivolity and light-headedness at all, all the more so in front of the common people, and not multiplying discretionary feasts with them - for indeed they said (Sanhedrin 52b), "To what is a Torah scholar compared before a common person? To a golden vessel. Once he speaks with him, he is like a silver vessel. Once he eats and drinks with him, he is like an earthenware vessel - once broken, it has no repair." And they must be honored so that awe of them falls upon people and their words be heeded. And they should not look too much toward outward appearances, but rather be among those who frequent the study house, for indeed they said (Eruvin 54a), "Why is Torah compared to a gazelle? To tell you, if a person makes himself like this gazelle, which appears and disappears, his learning will endure with him." And there is also a matter of desecration of the Name in this, for people will see it and likewise cause neglect of Torah study. And he should strive greatly that his work be done through others, and not demean himself by going to the grocer or the butcher shop or to carry a sack or basket - all according to what kind of person he is and the need of the hour, for the sake of Heaven he should maintain his own dignity. And likewise they must be careful of the honor of every person and honor the wealthy, for indeed Rabbi [Judah HaNasi] would honor the wealthy, and Rabbi Akiva would honor the wealthy (Eruvin 86a), even though they had no need of them, for they themselves were also wealthy - all the more so one who receives benefit from them must honor them and elevate them and give them thanks, and they deserve honor, since the King of the universe desired their honor and gave them the flow of wealth, and also for the mitzvot they perform with their wealth it is fitting to honor them.
Pele Yoetz 385:4: And these are matters that have no fixed measure - they should not demean themselves so far as to stand fully upright before them or to serve them and the like, things that are excessive, for then it passes out of the category of honor and enters the category of flattery, and everything should be done according to the custom of the region, in a manner that gives no cause for anyone to complain or speak ill of it. And if some person does not treat him with honor, or treats him disrespectfully, he should not be insistent about it at all, but should be truly humble and forgo his own honor. Let strangers praise him and not his own mouth, and let others insist on his honor and punish those who oppose him - not he himself, for it is disgraceful for a Torah scholar to claim his own honor and say, "I am a scholar's disciple." And the halachic authorities have written that there is no legal status of "Torah scholar" in this time in the strict sense, all the more so for people like us, who are but hyssop by the wall, so exceedingly have we become impoverished.
Pele Yoetz 385:5: Let him be careful of the honor of Torah scholars, especially in front of the common people - even to those younger than himself, he should honor and elevate them, and he should be very careful to guard against demeaning any Torah scholar, especially in front of the common people; scholars should not wound one another and speak ill of one another, for this constitutes a desecration of the Name, and people will say, "Prostitutes adorn one another, but Torah scholars wound one another - what is left for us, the common people?" And they must be exceedingly, exceedingly careful of every trace of prohibition, and especially in front of the common people they must be strict and sanctify themselves even in what is permitted to them, and not treat as forbidden what is truly permitted - in the manner of what they said (Berachot 19a), "An important person is different," for from the little that people see them being lenient, they will go on to be lenient in prohibitions far greater than these.
Pele Yoetz 385:6: And not only this, but Torah scholars themselves must be careful of all these things and even more, as explained in Maimonides' Laws of De'ot (chapter 5) and in other books, for the Torah scholar must fulfill every matter, "for this is Torah and this is its reward" - for it is not the exposition that is the essential thing, but the deed, and good conduct with people through good character traits and uprightness and the ways of proper social behavior, in a manner that finds favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man, for people learn from them as well, and there is a desecration of the Name if they do something improper, for people will say, "See, his sons and relatives and household, or those who attach themselves to the sage, do such and such - what is left for us?" And there is also disgrace to the sage himself, for people will say, "Before he rebukes the public, let him go and rebuke his own sons and household who behave improperly" - therefore they must be exceedingly careful. And we say every day, "Rabbi Elazar said in the name of Rabbi Chanina: Torah scholars increase peace in the world." Behold, then, let Torah scholars be careful to be among the disciples of Aaron, lovers of peace and pursuers of peace, loving people and drawing them near to the Torah, and let it begin with them that they have peace with everyone, and especially with their own wives and household members, and let them be among those who are insulted but do not insult. What more can I say - the matter is lengthy; the general principle is that they must guard against everything bad and keep and fulfill everything good, and be complete in character traits and in understanding, and know how to conduct themselves with every person according to his character, in an upright and good way, to a greater and stronger degree than any other person, in a manner that finds favor and good understanding in the eyes of God and man, so that the Name of Heaven not be desecrated through them, God forbid, but rather that they sanctify the Holy One of Jacob and the God of Israel, for indeed they said (Berachot 17a), "Happy is he whose labor is in Torah and who brings satisfaction to his Maker."
Pele Yoetz 386:1: Tehillim (Psalms) - Great is the merit of Psalms, and already our teacher, Rabbi [Chaim Yosef David] Azulai, in his book Yosef Tehillot, a pure man, gathered many good qualities said regarding the study of Psalms, producing a mighty work in brief. Our sages, of blessed memory, said (Yalkut Shimoni, Psalms 1) that King David, peace be upon him, prayed that he receive reward for them as one who occupies himself with the laws of afflictions and tents [i.e., difficult halachic topics]. And since King David prayed that it be considered as though he occupied himself with the laws of afflictions and tents, it appears that studying them is beneficial for the rectification of the brit (covenant), just as the disciples of the Ari wrote that studying the order of Purities is for the rectification of the blemish of the brit. Behold, then, it would not diminish a righteous man to study the entire book of Psalms every week, from one Sabbath to the next. And although the halachic authorities wrote that one who is capable of studying halachot and dialectics but instead occupies himself with Psalms is considered as engaging in neglect of Torah study relative to his own capacity, nevertheless, to study them once a week this was not said of, for there is a time for every desire. And how much more so if they are recited in public so that they be elevated - they rise more favorably than one who occupies himself privately with the laws of afflictions and tents. And it is written that one who is accustomed to the book of Psalms wards off all kinds of misfortune and evil occurrences from himself and from the members of his household and from his family and from all the people of his generation, and brings down upon them all kinds of abundance of blessings and good things and successes, and there is nothing to protect against harmful spirits like reciting Kaddish over the study of Psalms. And one who wishes to cling to Him, blessed be He, and to His praises, should cling to studying the book of Psalms. And there is a tradition from holy men of renown that one who has some pressing distress or trouble, or who is traveling on the road or crossing the sea or rivers, should recite the entire book of Psalms every day without interruption, with intention and humility, and he shall see wonders - this is tried and tested.
Pele Yoetz 386:2: And all these virtues and more than these belong to one who recites them properly, letter by letter, word by word, with a voice of song and thanksgiving and with a lowered voice of supplication, for he shall direct his spirit toward them and understand what he brings forth with his lips, for they are awesome prayers against the enemies and adversaries of the soul, to cut down the tyrants and to destroy all the thorns and briers, and great praises and songs to the One awesome in deeds - and the words are ancient and they are wondrous, perfect in knowledge, words of the living God that were spoken to King David through the holy spirit. And even though we do not know their depth and their loftiness, and there are places where one does not know what is being said, nevertheless the words are effective and bear fruit above, and "establish for us the work of our hands." But he must recite them with deliberation, without omissions and errors, unlike the custom of many fools among the people who recite them hastily with substitutions, omissions, and errors of all kinds - I fear for them that they incur sin in a place of mitzvah, if they are capable of reciting them properly, and their haste turns to evil for them; and we have already written about this above under the entry Rinah.
Pele Yoetz 386:3: And there is a custom among some fools that when they recite them in public and say one psalm for each person, some say and speak nothing except the psalm that pertains to them, to say it aloud, and meanwhile they speak idle words to one another or sit idle - these show that their recitation is not for the sake of Heaven, but only to display their wisdom, that they know how to recite a psalm of Tehillim, for if their recitation were for the sake of the mitzvah, what difference would it make whether in a whisper or aloud? And one to whom the Name has not granted understanding, or who has with him only the book of Psalms, should not refrain from repeating them even many times in a day and should not sit idle, for indeed our sages, of blessed memory, said (Tanna Devei Eliyahu, Bava Batra) that even if one reads and repeats and reads all day the verse (Genesis 36:22), "and Lotan's sister was Timna," he is given reward as though he occupied himself with the laws of afflictions and tents. And likewise one who has no book with him on the Sabbath in a shop or while walking on the road can study the psalms that are familiar to him by heart, or the Mishnayot familiar to him by heart, and repeat them even a thousand times, and he shall receive a good reward, pleasing to the Lord, as one who occupies himself with the laws of afflictions and tents. And indeed they said (Berachot 5b), "Both one who does much and one who does little [are equally rewarded], provided that he directs his heart to Heaven."
Pele Yoetz 387:1: Toldot (Offspring) - These are the pleasant offspring for a man, for this world and for the World to Come, if they are good offspring: the father of a righteous man shall greatly rejoice, and he who begets a wise son shall be glad in him in this world and shall delight in the abundance of his soul in the World to Come. Behold, then, a person is obligated to strive to establish offspring, and if he had children in his youth, he should strive to also have children in his old age, for he does not know which of them will turn out well, or from which of their offspring good will come - this one, or that one, or both together for good. And just as there is joy for a man in good offspring, so correspondingly, "a foolish son is a vexation to his father, and bitterness to her who bore him," and he shall be ashamed of them in this world. And it is already said (Bereishit Rabbah 44:9) that Abraham our father said, "If I am to have children who will anger You, it would be better for me to go childless." And so said King David, peace be upon him. And this shall be the comfort of the childless, that perhaps it is revealed before Heaven that unworthy children would come from them, and it is for their own good that this was done for them. Therefore let every person pray for this, that he have offspring, good sons and daughters, and let him strive to raise his sons in Torah and in service, and his daughters to be complete in character traits and in skills, and to marry them to Torah scholars or God-fearing men, and through this his heart shall rejoice and his glory shall exult.
Pele Yoetz 387:2: And behold, just as in the labors of the Sabbath there are primary categories (avot) and their derivatives (toldot), so in all the commandments there are primary categories, and from the primary categories come derivatives - that which comes forth from the pure is pure, and that which comes forth from the impure is impure; one mitzvah draws another mitzvah in its wake, and one transgression draws another transgression in its wake. And sometimes the primary category is hidden from the eye, yet the derivative testifies to the primary category, since a derivative cannot exist without a primary category - such as pride: it is hidden from the eyes of every living being, and everyone will say they have no pride, yet in truth none is free of it, whether much or little, for the derivatives of pride are anger and insistence on one's honor, and the derivatives of anger are curses, insults, and abuse, and their derivatives are hatred and rivalry, and their derivatives are that one sits and speaks against his brother, slandering his own mother's son and the like - and who is there so confident in his own heart that he is free of all these? And if there are no primary categories, from where would the derivatives come? Behold, then, let a person distance himself from transgressions and evil character traits and cling to the commandments and good character traits, for these things were not brought forth to teach about themselves alone, but they draw after them derivatives resembling themselves.
Pele Yoetz 387:3: And it is a well-known teaching of our sages, of blessed memory (Bereishit Rabbah 30:6), that the essential offspring of the righteous are good deeds, and their words are living and enduring - and this accords well with their teaching, of blessed memory (Avot 4:11), that one who performs a single mitzvah acquires for himself an advocate, which is an angel created from that mitzvah. And it is better to beget an angel than to beget a son of flesh and blood who is destined to sin, and the angel that becomes his advocate benefits his soul more than a son of flesh and blood benefits him. Therefore, happy is the man who fears the Lord and delights greatly in His commandments - and when he sees how much the childless toil to establish offspring, let him reason a fortiori on that very day how much more he must toil to establish the essential offspring, which are good deeds; for what do actual offspring give or add, if not that he thinks that through them he will find rest for his soul - and this is doubly doubtful, especially in these generations, when there are few children of true stature who bring elevation to the souls of their fathers - would that they cause them no grief instead! Behold, then, it is good for a man that his righteousness go before him as a good advocate on his behalf, as it is written (Psalms 49:19), "and they praise you when you do well for yourself."
Pele Yoetz 388:1:
Tosefet Shabbat and Tosefet Yom HaKippurim (Adding to the Sabbath and Yom Kippur)
Our Maker commanded us regarding these to add from the weekday onto the holy day, and this was said not merely to teach about themselves, but to teach a general principle for all - that a person is obligated to add to the commandments of the Torah. And it has already come explained (Leviticus 18:30), "And you shall keep My charge" - "make a guard for My charge" (Yevamot 21a), that a person is obligated to flee from a hundred gates of the permitted so as not to enter even one gate of the forbidden. And it is likewise written (Leviticus 19:2), "You shall be holy," and our sages, of blessed memory, explained (Yevamot 20a), "You shall be set apart - sanctify yourself even in what is permitted to you." And a person is obligated to go on adding holiness day by day - his eye shall not be satisfied, just as one who loves money is never satisfied with money - and this adding indicates that he serves out of love, for the many waters of the vanities of this world cannot extinguish love. And the books of ethics have already written that the goodness and virtue of adding lies in adding to the essential thing, not that the addition should nullify the essential thing - so that a scale and balance of judgment are needed, for sometimes one should add, and sometimes the nullification of Torah is its fulfillment; both one who does much and one who does little [are equally rewarded], provided that he directs his heart to Heaven.
Pele Yoetz 389:1: Toke'a (Shofar Blower) - It is stated in the holy Zohar, portion Vayikra, that Rabbi Elazar said, "I saw my father on the days of Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, that he did not wish to hear the prayer from just any person, but rather only from one who had spent three days beforehand in purifying himself, and all the more so regarding the blowing of the shofar, for he would not accept the blowing of a person who was not skilled in the mystery of the blowing." Further there it says that on this day the people need to look to a person who is complete in all things, who knows the ways of the holy King, who knows the honor of the King, that he should intercede for them on this day and summon the sound of the shofar throughout all the worlds with intention of heart, with wisdom, with will, with completeness, so that judgment be removed from the world through him. Woe to those whose messenger is not found to be fitting as required, for then the sins of the world come to be remembered because of him - this is what is written (Leviticus 4:3), "If the anointed priest shall sin," for he is the emissary of all Israel, causing the guilt of the people, for judgment rests upon them; but when the emissary is righteous as required, happy are the people, for all judgments are removed from them through him. This is the essence of the words of the holy Zohar.
Pele Yoetz 389:2: And when this language is seen, the heart of the worshippers would melt and the hands of the shofar blowers of our time would grow weak, for we have grown so exceedingly poor that we lack all good. In any case, an obligation rests upon us to choose the lesser evil, for we have only the shofar blowers and worshippers of our own days, and we already lament this every Monday and Thursday, saying, "Men of faith have perished," etc., "those fit to appease You are gone, we have searched the four corners and found no remedy, so we have returned to You in the shame of our faces." But we must lie down in our shame, and let our disgrace cover us, and let us grieve and be exceedingly humbled and crushed over this, and let us do what is in our power to do, and let us select the best in our community to be the shofar blowers and worshippers. And let each person flee from entering this contest, for if he is not found fitting as required, the sins of the world will come to be remembered because of him. Therefore, in a place where there are worthy men, one should not strive to be the man himself; but if he finds himself in a place with no other worthy men, so that he is compelled to be the one, in any case let the shofar blowers and worshippers do what is in their power to do, and let them precede by engaging in fasting and a program of repentance for at least three days before Rosh Hashanah, and let them offer prayer in advance for the trouble, that their prayers and blowings be favorably received, and that the world not be punished because of them. And when they stand to serve in the Name of the Name, let them clothe themselves in dread; let awe and fear fall upon them, and let them cling to their Maker with great humility, with a broken and crushed heart, for this alone remains for us to rely upon, as it is written (Psalms 51:19), "A broken and crushed heart, O God, You will not despise."
Pele Yoetz 389:3: And this is a great principle for the prayers of all days, for the community and for the individual, all the more so for the prayers of these mighty days - for given the greatness and essence of our sins and the smallness of our worth and the shortness of our understanding, if God should bring us into judgment, we would surely perish and be lost, God forbid; we have nothing to rely upon except His attribute and our own poverty, that our Father in Heaven deal charitably with us according to our poverty and according the greatness of His mercies and kindnesses and the ten gifts of His hand. And behold, every single Jew needs this quality, that he humble himself like hyssop and that his heart be subdued in prayers, and that the poor man speak supplications like a poor man begging at the door - perhaps there is hope. And all the more so must the prayer leaders be careful of this, and they need great strength so as not to turn to reckless intentions, calculating to show the nations and the officials their beauty, as if to say, "See now how well I blow the shofar, or how I pray with pleasant speech and a weeping voice" - and if this is bad and bitter at all times, all the more so on these days, for it is destructive of souls, may the Merciful One save us; therefore let them strengthen themselves with pure thoughts to push away these evil thoughts and to cling to their Maker with great humility - perhaps God will be entreated.
Pele Yoetz 389:4: And even if he does not know how to direct the mystical intentions, as in this orphaned generation where those of true stature who know how to direct them are few, for the matters are ancient and deep - who can fathom it? - nevertheless it is good for a man to look into the writings in which the intentions are recorded, and to study in the holy book of the Zohar the passages that speak of the mystery of the shofar blasts, so that he know and his heart understand that there are deep secrets, and let him think of them at the time of the blasts, gazing at them like a blind man peering through a window, and he should not refrain from studying and directing simple intentions that are within everyone's grasp, and let his heart cry out to his Father that these matters be rectified through his blasts in the supernal place, as though he had directed all the intentions along with the blasts of those who know and are attuned to the wisdom of Rashbi and all the holy ones - and the Lord in His mercies does not despise or loathe the affliction of the afflicted, and does not hide His face from him, and hears the sound of the shofar-blast of His people Israel with mercy.
Pele Yoetz 389:5: And behold, the commandment of blowing the shofar is one of the six hundred and thirteen commandments, and it is an important commandment that recurs from time to time, and it comes as a remembrance before the Name for our good all our days, to keep us alive. And if for all the commandments one must strive to fulfill them properly, with full completeness, all the more so this commandment, at this time and season when the King sits upon the throne of judgment - this comes out first: one must strive greatly to blow a ram's horn shofar, for according to all halachic authorities a ram's horn is the preferred choice for this mitzvah. And according to Maimonides, one does not fulfill his obligation with a horn of another kind at all, only with a ram's horn. And although we follow the majority opinion, nevertheless one should be concerned for the individual minority opinion, and a God-fearing person should fulfill his obligation according to all views - and this applies to all commandments, all the more so and with even greater force to this commandment. And the Rabbi, author of Ya'arot Devash, already wrote a parable on this: if all the physicians unanimously said regarding a patient whose life is in danger that a certain medicine coming from overseas is the best for the cure, but that a medicine from other lands is also somewhat effective, and one skilled and expert physician said that nothing helps at all except the medicine from overseas - certainly one would heed the words of the expert physician, since all agree that it is the best, and one would run without tiring to obtain it. And if this is how people act regarding the healing of the body, all the more so regarding the healing of the soul. And the shofar blower must be expert in the laws of the blasts, how long each one must be extended. And he must be exceedingly careful not to err, for indeed they said (Berachot 34b), "A prayer leader who errs is a bad sign for those who sent him." Therefore he should be careful not to frighten the people of Israel.
Pele Yoetz 389:6: And it is well known what is said in the holy Zohar: "Any commandment that is not performed with awe and love does not fly upward." And regarding this commandment, there is no person among Israel who does not feel some stirring of awe - "Shall a shofar be blown in a city, and the people not tremble?" However, it is known that there is fear and there is fear: the fear of punishment is called in the holy Zohar "the bad fear," and one must arouse instead the fear of grandeur, for our Lord is great and mighty, and His greatness is unfathomable. Go and learn: on Rosh Hashanah all who come into the world, the upper beings and the lower beings, pass before Him like sheep in single file, in a single moment, and all are surveyed in a single glance, whether for good or for less than good; and the heavenly host, who know somewhat more of the Creator's greatness than we do, tremble and shake with great commotion, as much as they can bear, since their bodies are fire, and a river of fire flows forth from their sweat due to the greatness of the commotion, to the point that it is said that it is out of the Name's compassion for us that we were not given to comprehend His greatness, for if we were to comprehend it even as the least of the heavenly host does, our bodies would be ground and turned to ash from the excess of dread. Over this a person should tremble and be seized with fear - how has he caused grief and anger to such a King, so exalted and lofty, awesome and terrible, and what will he do when God rises to judgment, as on this day, when the King establishes the earth in justice? Such and such things should he deepen in pure thoughts, to arouse himself to fear the honored and awesome Name. But he must also arouse himself in love, taking to heart the teaching of our sages, of blessed memory, that whoever has a case before a king of flesh and blood wears black and wraps himself in black; but we, on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur, wear white and wrap ourselves in white, because we are confident in our Father in Heaven that He will bring forth our judgment favorably, for He has loved us with an everlasting love and a great love. Go and learn: who is like the Lord our God, who provides the remedy before the wound, saying, "When you sin before Me, do such and such, and I will be reconciled with you and forgive you" - and not only that, but these very blasts are also counted as a mitzvah, and He establishes for us a good reward for them. Is there a palate so sweet as this? Is there one so complete in traits and understanding and every kind of perfection as the Lord our God? And not only this, but through the speech of our lips and the breath that goes out of our mouth, He builds His chambers in heaven, and it becomes a source of great satisfaction to our Father in Heaven - happy is the one born of woman who has merited this; happy are we, how good is our portion! Such and such things should he deepen in pure thoughts to arouse love, and let his eye weep bitterly while his heart rejoices, worries, and trusts.
Pele Yoetz 389:7: And one must also take to heart to know what this commandment is and what reason there is for it, and not to perform it as a commandment learned by rote from others. And behold, the plain reason given for the commandment that the Name commanded us to blow the shofar is to recall for us the binding of Isaac our father, for whom a ram was substituted as a favorable atonement, and our holy ancestors, may their merit protect us. And this is included in the general recollection of how much we must love the Creator with all our soul, and all the more so with our body and our money, for all that a man has he will give for his life. And this is why it is called "shofar," for the Holy One, blessed be He, said, "Improve (shapru) your deeds" (Vayikra Rabbah 29:6).
Pele Yoetz 389:8: And the reason for the order of the blasts is that the Holy One, blessed be He, commanded to blow three teruot, and before and after each teruah a plain blast (tekiah) - and here we enter a matter of doubt, because the Aramaic translation of "teruah" is "yabava," meaning wailing, and there are three kinds of weeping in the world: there is one who sighs sigh after sigh, and through this is aroused to weep with great wailing; there is one who weeps only with a broken sigh; and there is one who begins immediately with a great wailing. Therefore, corresponding to these three kinds of weeping, three orders were instituted: Tashrat, corresponding to the first kind we mentioned; Tashat, corresponding to the second kind; Tarat, corresponding to the third kind - this is, in brief, the reason for these orders according to the plain sense. We thus learn that the mitzvah of the day is to be aroused to a sound of weeping and wailing - but one must inform the people why they should weep, for if you tell someone to weep and he finds no reason to weep, the man will be alarmed and say, "Let my enemies who wish me ill weep - why should I weep, and for what should I weep? No evil has befallen me." But regarding this, surely it is fitting for us to weep, fitting for us to lament, with great weeping and bitter mourning, for our eyes have grown dark from seeing the greatness of our own wickedness, and our heart has become dull as fat, and we are like a sick person whose illness has become so severe upon him that he no longer feels his sickness, and he goes mad and says he is healthy and wants to rise and flee from his bed - so is this matter, that we are so sunk in the mire of our sins that we do not feel them, and our way is upright in our own eyes, and our sins withhold the good from us, and we have gone from evil to evil, and our iniquities have separated between us and our Father in Heaven, to the point that we cannot direct our minds to fear the honored and awesome Name as required, even at this very time and season - this is an evil greater than any other, that we are like the dead while yet alive. And if a man weeps bitterly over the death of a son, his only son, even though he cannot bring him back, all the more so must one weep over the death of his own soul, for through weeping perhaps it shall live - and just as a man would weep over his dead if he could revive him through his weeping, so let us give voice to weeping, perhaps God will be entreated for us and revive us again, and bring us up again from the depths of the earth. And as they said in the holy Zohar, "Behold, a weeping youth" - this refers to Israel, as it is written (Hosea 11:1), "For Israel was a youth, and I loved him" - as soon as he began to weep, immediately "she had compassion on him."
Pele Yoetz 389:9: And it is true that our hearts also ache over this: that we cannot weep with great weeping as befits our hearts and as is fitting for us, due to the blindness of our eyes - for if we merited even a little that our eyes be opened, and we saw the greatness and essence of our sins, and what we have caused through them: the exile of the Shechinah and the destruction of the Temple, and the corruption of the channels of divine flow, and the grief of the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, and the grief of the upper and lower worlds, and blemish in all the worlds, and the delay of the Messiah, and many such evils that we have caused - so that it is said of us (Proverbs 17:25), "A foolish son is a vexation to his father, and bitterness to her who bore him" - if we saw and felt even a little of all this, it would be fitting for us to weep with truly great weeping, until our very souls departed, like the deed of Rabbi Elazar ben Durdaya (Avodah Zarah 17a), whose soul departed in weeping, and he was found fit for the life of the World to Come. Would that our heads were water and our eyes a fountain of tears, and we could weep day and night until our souls departed.
Pele Yoetz 389:10: And it is already said of our teacher the Ari, of blessed memory, that he would weep greatly on these mighty days, and he said that whoever is not aroused to weeping on these days, it is a sign that his soul is not purified. Woe to us - for although we need no signs, since what is well known needs no proof, and we know for certain that our way before the Name was like the impurity of a menstruating woman - nevertheless there is also a clear sign in our hands, spoken by a holy mouth: that we are unable to bring forth a tear except after great forcing of the soul, and perhaps some tear will emerge; and had we merited that our souls be purified, streams of water would flow from our eyes without ceasing out of our grief, so that the world not burn in flames of righteous indignation, and there be no grief and bitterness to the Holy One, blessed be He, on our account - as stated in the Idra Kadisha, that Rashbi grieved over this, and what shall we answer after him? And so it would have been fitting that our couch melt with our tears when we remember the dread of Rabbi Yochanan ben Zakkai over the day of judgment (Berachot 28b) - and what shall we answer after them? Of this it is said (Lamentations 3:39), "Why should a living man complain," etc. And if we saw and felt all this and more, it would be fitting that we bring down tears like a river; but now we do not feel any of this, and we cannot grieve over it and weep properly as required, because our souls are not purified. Rather, let us be strong and strengthen ourselves regarding this, to feel complete remorse for all that we have sinned and for all that we have fallen short in the service of the blessed Name, and let Israel say, "What has passed has passed; from now on we shall think well of ourselves," and let us strive with all our strength to cleanse our hands from every evil thing and from every trace of prohibition, and to keep and do and fulfill every good thing, and may the Lord God help us, and let us give voice in a voice of weeping with great humility, in the manner of what is written (Psalms 6:9), "Depart from me, all workers of iniquity, for the Lord has heard the voice of my weeping" - the voice, precisely - perhaps God will be entreated for us and His mercies shall stir for us, and He shall remove from us only this death by which we die while yet alive, and inscribe us in the book of good life.
Pele Yoetz 390:1: Tishah B'Av (The Ninth of Av) - The Ninth of Av is the day that the Lord called for weeping and lamentation. And if on all other days, when the destruction of the Temple is mentioned, such as in reciting Tikkun Chatzot and the like, it is fitting to arouse weeping and mourning, all the more so on this day, when surely the grief of Heaven is great, Rachel weeping for her children, and the Lord shall roar from on high and give forth His voice from His holy dwelling, roaring mightily over His habitation, more and more than on other days. Behold, then, even though through our sins our eyes have grown dark from seeing the evil we have caused through our sins, and we cannot grieve and weep and bring down tears like a river as would be fitting and proper for us, as we have written above under the entry Avelut, in any case let us do what is in our power to do. And let a man imagine in his mind as though in his ears he hears the sound of thousands upon thousands and myriads upon myriads of holy camps, weeping aloud with great wailing and a great and bitter outcry, and let his heart writhe within him over having caused such great grief to his Father and Mother, the Holy One, blessed be He, and His Shechinah, and to all the heavenly host - the righteous and the pious and the angels and the seraphim and the ofanim - perhaps his heart will be aroused to be embittered in weeping, and his tears will fall; and in any case, if he cannot weep and shed tears, let him recite the Lamentations (Kinot) in a voice of weeping, and let him sit alone the entire night and day with a sorrowful face, until all who see him recognize that he is more bitter and sorrowful than one whose dead lies before him, and let him not turn his mind from mourning. And accordingly, they forbade playing with a child, and even engaging in Torah study they forbade, because it is written (Psalms 19:9), "The precepts of the Lord are upright, rejoicing the heart" - all the more so is other frivolity and light-headedness forbidden. And likewise they forbade the drinking of tobacco. And in the time of the great sage Kneset HaGedolah there was a man who smoked tobacco after midday and he excommunicated him.
Pele Yoetz 390:2: And now, through our sins, there are many fools among the people who do not know what Tisha B'Av is, and the Lamentations have become to them like songs of entertainment or a matter for mockery and jesting, and immediately upon leaving the synagogue they go strolling, and many are lax about removing their shoes, coming in shoes all the way to their seats in the synagogue - and there are some who, when they arrive in the morning at the synagogue, remove them from their feet, but after leaving the synagogue pay no attention at all. And there are those who wash their hands and face as on every other day because they do not know the prohibition, and there are those who are careful only until midday, but after midday it seems to them that everything is permitted, and they increase in joy, saying, "Nachamu has already come," and they wash their faces, hands, and feet and put on leather shoes. And it is fitting for those who know the proper timing of things to caution them not to transgress the words of the sages, for their judgment is our disgrace and our shame and our humiliation, that we are like a fool or like a very sick man whose relative has died and he does not feel it - so we do not feel grief in our souls over the destruction of the house of our holiness and our glory and over all that we have caused through our sins. At the very least let us do what is in our hands to show mourning and sorrow and to observe the laws as required - namely, that the entire day, until the stars come out, eating, drinking, and washing are forbidden, and it is not permitted to wash even for the morning hand-washing, or when leaving the bathroom, except up to the knuckles of the fingers; and likewise greeting others is forbidden, and for us it is forbidden to say "buenos dias" (good day) as some are accustomed to do. And it is forbidden to perform work the entire day, and it is good for a man to sit alone. And the wearing of shoes is forbidden by law until the stars come out, anywhere within a Jewish quarter - though there are those who are lenient when walking in a gentile street, even though this is not the accepted practice, and it is not the way of the pious to transgress the words of the sages for fear of the mockery of the complacent, for in any case we are already "a disgrace to our neighbors, mockery and derision to those around us" (Psalms 44:14, 79:4). But in any case, those who walk in a gentile street wearing leather shoes have something to rely upon; but as soon as they enter a Jewish quarter, if they do not remove their shoes, they have nothing to rely upon and are committing a transgression. And likewise it is forbidden to drink tobacco, and every kind of play and joy is forbidden the entire day. There is no leniency even after midday except to sit on a bench, for until midday one must sit on the ground. And it is already said in the Talmud (Ta'anit 29a) that there was a sage who said that if he had been present at that time, he would have established the fast on the tenth, since the main burning of the Temple was on the tenth - what joy is there in this? And the holy people of Israel, upon hearing that there is a prohibition in the matter, should not transgress the words of the sages with contemptuous disregard; and to the extent that they do transgress, it is because, for the entire people, it is done unwittingly, and the good Name shall atone for it. And whoever mourns for Jerusalem as much as he can shall merit to see her joy. And this is what every person must have as his whole intent and aim: to fulfill each matter in its proper time - in a time of sorrow, sorrow, and in a time of joy, joy - and through this shall Israel rejoice in its Maker.
